This morning, the sky touched my roof.
Every street in the world holds up its own piece of sky.
Whoever lets go, it comes down on their street.
Nobody knows what's on top of it.
Our sky is blue, and hard, and close enough to hit with a rock.
On my street, it's forty feet up.
Every street has one pole, thick as a tower, with a crank at the bottom.
Every hour, a bell rings, and the whole street turns the crank. One turn.
Weddings happen under the pole, so the vows hold too.
Babies sleep in the crank house. It's the last thing to fall.
We learn cranking before counting.
Our sun is a white circle on the sky. It never moves. It never sets.
On every pole, we painted the same three words. Hold it up.
I'm the greaser. I climb every pole on our side of town with a bucket.
A dry screw slips. A slipping screw drops a street.
My best friend Ollie is eight. He rides on my shoulders while I work.
At every pole, he points straight up. Higher? he asks.
One day, I say.
Overseer Kell lives on the Hill. Up there, the sky is so high, they fly kites.
Kell decides where the poles stand.
Every year, the sky sinks a little lower.
And every year, Kell needs one more pole for the Hill. He takes it from a street like mine.
Our street had three poles when I was born. Now it has one.
Last spring, I skipped Pole Nine. Just once. Ollie wanted to race.
That night, its screw slipped.
The sky came down on Tanner Street, slow, like a lid on a pot.
Forty houses. Flat.
Kell walked down from the Hill and looked at the flat street. Somebody didn't grease, he said.
Everyone looked at me.
But I went back to Pole Nine. The screw was still greasy. And there was a fresh cut in it. From a saw.
The next week, Pole Nine was standing on the Hill.
Last night, Kell's men took our last spare pole.
This morning, the sky sat down on our chimneys.
We cranked until the crank snapped. The roofs started to crack.
Nobody climbs the pole. It's the one thing you never do. I climbed it.
Forty feet. The sky was right above my head.
Then something fell on my face. From above. It was dirt.
I pushed my grease knife into the sky. It isn't stone. It's wood, painted blue.
Under me, the street cracked. Eight feet left. Seven.
I cut a hole, and pushed my head through.
Sunlight. Real sunlight. And wheat, all the way to the edge of the world.
Our sky is somebody's farm.
On a ladder from the Hill, Kell's men were spreading more dirt. Right over my street.
Every year, the sky gets heavier, because every year, they plant more.
We were never holding up the sky. We were holding up their fields.
I climbed down and told my street. Nobody believed me, until I opened my hand. Wheat.
So for the first time in history, a street let go on purpose.
We carried the babies out first. Then we stepped back.
The sky came down on our houses, and Kell's field came down with it.
Wheat poured into our street like gold rain. And through the hole, the sun. The real one.
Up on the edge, Kell stared down at the hole in his farm.
We lost every house we had.
Ollie climbed onto my shoulders, and pointed at the real sky. Higher? he asked.
I lifted him up. That sky, nobody holds up.
